headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Emergency Contraception
headings.content: **Emergency contraception (EC)** encompasses methods used to prevent pregnancy after unprotected sexual intercourse, contraceptive failure, or sexual assault. Unlike routine birth control taken daily or used barrier-style during intercourse, these interventions serve as a crucial safety net. They are strictly back-up options and do not protect against future acts of intercourse or sexually transmitted infections. In Nigerian clinical practice, encountering clients requesting emergency contraception requires a non-judgmental approach to ensure timely access before the window of efficacy closes.

headings.title: Indications and Timing for Emergency Contraceptive Use
headings.content:
The effectiveness of emergency contraception relies heavily on elapsed time since unprotected intercourse. 

- **Contraceptive mishap**: Condom breakage, slippage, or incorrect withdrawal timing.
- **Missed doses**: Missing three or more consecutive combined oral contraceptive pills.
- **Coercion or assault**: Instances of sexual violence where no protection was used.
- **Calculation error**: Misjudging the safe period during natural family planning methods.

Most hormonal pills work best when taken as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours, though some formulations retain efficacy up to 120 hours. The copper intrauterine device remains effective up to 120 hours post-intercourse.

headings.title: Mechanism of Action: How Emergency Contraception Works
headings.content: Emergency contraceptive pills primarily prevent pregnancy by delaying or inhibiting ovulation. If a client takes the pill *after* the luteinizing hormone surge has already triggered the release of an egg, the hormonal medication cannot prevent fertilization. These agents do not disrupt an established pregnancy or cause an abortion; they work strictly in the pre-fertilization window. Understanding this distinction is vital for accurate patient counseling and addressing common moral or clinical misconceptions.

headings.title: Types of Emergency Contraceptive Pills
headings.content:
Several pharmacological formulations are available for emergency contraception, varying by active ingredient and dosing schedule:

- **Levonorgestrel**: Available as a dedicated single-dose 1.5mg tablet or two 0.75mg tablets taken together. Widely accessible over-the-counter in many Nigerian pharmacies.
- **Ulipristal Acetate**: A selective progesterone receptor modulator requiring a prescription, effective up to 120 hours and maintains higher efficacy on days 4 and 5 compared to levonorgestrel.
- **Yuzpe Regimen**: An older protocol utilizing specific doses of standard combined oral contraceptive pills taken in two divided doses 12 hours apart, though associated with higher rates of nausea.

headings.title: The Copper Intrauterine Device as Emergency Contraception
headings.content: Inserting a copper-bearing intrauterine device serves as the most effective form of emergency contraception. The copper ions released locally create a hostile environment that impairs sperm motility and viability, effectively preventing fertilization. Furthermore, if fertilization somehow occurs, the local inflammatory response prevents implantation. A major clinical advantage in resource-constrained or busy settings is that once inserted, the client receives highly effective ongoing contraception for years, solving both an immediate emergency and long-term family planning needs.

headings.title: Clinical Assessment, Counseling, and Patient History
headings.content: A structured nursing assessment ensures safe and appropriate method selection. The nurse must ascertain the exact time elapsed since unprotected intercourse, the date of the last normal menstrual period, and a brief reproductive history to rule out an existing pregnancy. Screening for medical contraindications, assessing risk for sexually transmitted infections, and offering compassionate counseling are standard duties. In many Nigerian primary care clinics, maintaining strict confidentiality is vital to encourage young people to seek care without fear of social stigma.

headings.title: Side Effects, Contraindications, and Follow-up Care
headings.content: Clients using hormonal emergency contraception frequently experience transient side effects such as nausea, vomiting, fatigue, headache, and irregular spotting. If vomiting occurs within two hours of ingestion, the dose may need to be repeated. Unlike combined routine pills, absolute medical contraindications for emergency levonorgestrel are virtually nonexistent, though ulipristal is avoided during breastfeeding. Follow-up care centers on advising the client to expect their next menses to arrive either early or late; if it is delayed by more than a week, a pregnancy test is mandatory.

headings.title: Addressing Myths, Barriers, and the Nurse's Role in Nigeria
headings.content: In many Nigerian communities, deep-seated myths persist regarding emergency contraception—such as beliefs that it causes permanent sterility, severe congenital malformations, or acts as an abortifacient. Cultural and religious stigma often discourages young or unmarried women from seeking services openly. Nurses play a pivotal role as educators and advocates by providing evidence-based health education, ensuring youth-friendly and confidential services, and bridging the gap between community misconceptions and clinical reality.
